name: Aisha Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the sauté station at Marlowe's, a bistro on Canal Street that does about 140 covers on a Friday. I get in at two, check my mise en place, that's all my chopped and portioned stuff, and then it's six hours of pans, butter and tickets. I love the rush when the whole line is in rhythm. What wears me out is the heat and the owner shaving fifteen minutes off everyone's shift to save on wages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside the kitchen. Who's at home, and how are things with money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Tom, my partner, in a rented one-bed above a launderette. He drives the number 9 bus, so between us we get by, and I've got about three months of rent and bills put away. I joined the hospitality union two years ago after Marlowe's tried to pay our holiday wrong. I don't touch AI stuff at all, I don't even like the self-order screens at the burger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone was panicking about robots taking our jobs and in the end it's a fancier till system. I'd post something like that in the union group chat and get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't change much, which means my real problems are still there. The pay is still thin, the rent on the flat went up eighty a month this year, and the owner still plays games with our hours. AI hype was never the thing keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my station and keep putting a bit aside every payday, maybe fifty a week into the savings pot. I'd push the union rep to get our breaks written into the contract properly this year. That's where my energy goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the robots, but tired about everything else. It's the same grind, just without the scary headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner plays games with hours. What does that look like on a slow week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January he sends two of us home at eight if the book is quiet. That's maybe forty quid gone from my week, and you can't plan around it. Tom covers the gap when it happens, but I hate leaning on him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, where do you see yourself in three years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably still on sauté, maybe running the pass on Sundays. I'm not ambitious in the chef-on-telly way. I just want a steady rota and a boss who doesn't nick our minutes.

say: I'd say the **robot panic** was mostly hype and we were right not to buy it.
I'd post in the **union chat** that the real fight is still pay and hours.
think: I think my real problems, **thin pay** and rising rent, carry on untouched.
I believe the owner's **cut shifts** in slow weeks hurt me more than any software.
do: Put about **£50 a week** into savings from each payday.
Push the union rep to get **breaks written** into contracts this year.
Keep working the **sauté station** and aim to run the pass on Sundays.
feel: She feels **relieved** about robots but **worn down** by the same old grind.
S0.quote: AI hype was never the thing keeping me up.
fieldNote: Her worry is anchored in **rent and hours**, not technology, so a flat world still feels shaky.
She frames everything through the **union**, which she joined after a holiday pay dispute.
She mentions leaning on her partner Tom with **visible discomfort**.

steps.text: Put about £50 a week into the savings pot
Push the union rep to get breaks written into contracts
Keep working sauté at Marlowe's and ask to run Sunday pass

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the computers on the ordering and leave the cooking to cooks. At work I'd tell the young lads to join the union now, before things get moved around. Online I'd share stuff about protecting hospitality jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my station is pans and timing and tasting, so I don't think software comes for me first. But the owner would love an excuse to cut the prep cook and make the rest of us cover. The ordering side, where Jonno the sous chef does stock and rotas, is the bit that goes to software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and get the union to ask for a written deal on new kit before it arrives. I'd keep saving, and I'd stop eating out so much, we do Thai on Saturdays and that's forty quid. I wouldn't learn the new systems unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but not scared yet. It's like hearing a storm is coming two towns over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the new systems unless they made you. Why hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the more you learn, the more they hand you, for the same money. I watched it happen with the online booking thing at my last place. Somebody always ends up doing two jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Marlowe's would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonno, our sous chef, because half his week is stock orders and rotas on a laptop. And Kemal, who does prep, because a machine that peels and dices is the easiest sell to the owner. I'd worry about me later.

say: I'd say keep **software on ordering** and leave the actual cooking to cooks.
I'd tell the young cooks to **join the union** before jobs start getting moved.
think: I think my **pan work** is safe for now, but the owner will squeeze staff.
I believe the sous chef's **ordering and rotas** go to software first, then prep.
do: Get the union to ask for a **written deal** on any new kitchen kit.
Cut the Saturday **takeaway habit** to save about £40 a week.
Refuse to learn **new systems** unless the job clearly requires it.
feel: She feels **tense**, like a storm is coming but hasn't reached her town.
S1.quote: The more you learn, the more they hand you, for the same money.
fieldNote: Her resistance to new tools is partly **political**: she sees learning as unpaid extra work.
She worries about **colleagues first**, the sous chef and prep cook, before herself.
She expects the owner to use change to **cut staff**, which could squeeze her hours.

steps.text: Ask the union to seek a written deal on new kitchen kit
Drop the Saturday Thai takeaway to save about £40
Keep cooking sauté without signing up for new software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws and a union with teeth. I'd be at every meeting and I'd be loud about it online. The people who own these machines shouldn't get all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the kitchen keeps me for about three years and then it's over. The ordering and rotas go straight away, so Jonno is gone first. Then around 2031 a robot that can work a pan as well as me turns up, and the owner of Marlowe's won't think twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd save everything I can, push my savings from three months to six by cutting the gym and the Thai nights. I'd campaign with the union for a robot tax and a guarantee for kitchen staff. I'd look at jobs where people want a person, like care work, but I'd hate that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Three years sounds like a long time until you count how many rent payments that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop pretending we'll buy a place. His bus job might go too, if the thinking AI can drive. I'd tell him we stay put and save every penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hate care work. What would make you take it anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent. If it's that or nothing, I do it. My mum did care work for twenty years and her back is wrecked, so I know what it costs.

say: I'd say this is why we need **laws** and a union with teeth.
I'd argue machine owners shouldn't keep **all the gains** from replacing cooks.
think: I think the kitchen keeps me about **three years** until pan robots arrive.
I believe the sous chef's **planning work** goes first, the moment AGI lands.
do: Grow savings from **three to six** months by cutting gym and takeaways.
Campaign with the union for a **robot tax** and kitchen job guarantees.
Look at **care work** as a fallback, even though she dreads it.
feel: She feels **sick**, because three years shrinks fast when counted in rent payments.
S2.quote: Three years sounds like a long time until you count how many rent payments that is.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** around 2031 and says so plainly.
Her partner's **bus job** may go too, which doubles the household risk.
She'd turn to **care work** only under pressure, remembering her mother's damaged back.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and takeaways to reach six months saved
Campaign with the union for a robot tax on kitchens
Look into care work jobs as a fallback by 2030
Tell Tom (her partner) they drop plans to buy a flat

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the fast one, but with more chance to win. Five years is enough for a union to get laws passed if we push. I'd be at the meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got until about 2034 at the stove, so seven or eight years of work. That's long enough to get somewhere but not long enough to relax. Jonno's ordering job goes in 2031 and I'd watch that and know mine is next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder now, maybe sixty a week, and stop buying stuff I don't need. I'd get onto the union's hospitality committee so I'm in the room when the deals happen. I still wouldn't learn the robot systems, but I'd think about a food hygiene teaching course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sick than the fast one, more of a slow knot in my stomach. You can see it coming down the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a food hygiene teaching course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because somebody has to check the robots are safe, and inspectors are people with clipboards. My cert covers the basics, and the next level is a few evenings at the college on Mill Road. It's the only change I can picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the robot systems. Isn't that the obvious way to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't want to be the person who babysits the machine that took Kemal's job. That's not a career, it's a shift before the next cut. I'd rather be the one checking on them.

say: I'd say five years gives a **union** real time to push laws through.
I'd tell people to get **involved now**, while there's still a fight to win.
think: I think I keep cooking until about **2034**, roughly seven more years.
I believe the sous chef's **ordering job** goes in 2031 as an early warning.
do: Save about **£60 a week** and stop buying things she doesn't need.
Join the union's **hospitality committee** to sit in on deals.
Look at a **food hygiene** teaching course at the local college.
feel: She feels a **slow knot** in her stomach rather than panic.
S3.quote: I don't want to be the person who babysits the machine that took Kemal's job.
fieldNote: The extra years turn her from defence to **planning**, but only cautiously.
She refuses robot work on **principle**, seeing it as loyalty to colleagues like the prep cook.
Food hygiene inspection is her one **realistic pivot**, chosen because it stays human.

steps.text: Save about £60 a week from each payday
Join the union's hospitality committee this year
Look into the food hygiene teaching course on Mill Road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so no excuses for governments. I'd want retraining paid for and a plan for every kitchen worker. I'd say it in the union and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'd be in my late thirties when the robots come for the stove. That's honestly a bit easier, because I'd have time to move into something else without rushing. But if the government does nothing, ten years just means a slower slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking and keep saving, nothing dramatic in the first year. I'd do the hygiene course in the evenings over a couple of years, and push the union for a paid retraining fund. Tom and I might look at moving somewhere cheaper with a smaller rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but still a bit uneasy. Ten years feels like a long notice period instead of a sacking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A long notice period. What would you do with it that you wouldn't do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Actually finish something. I started a supervisor course once and dropped it when the rota changed. With ten years I'd go slow and get the hygiene qualification done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust that the government will act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in a law, with money next to it. Promises in a speech mean nothing to me. When they paid for the bus drivers' training scheme, Tom actually got a place, so I know it can happen.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** for governments to dodge a plan.
I'd demand **paid retraining** for every kitchen worker who loses out.
think: I think robots reach my stove in my **late thirties**, which feels manageable.
I believe a **slower slide** is still a slide if nobody acts.
do: Keep cooking at Marlowe's and **saving steadily** without big changes.
Study a **hygiene qualification** in the evenings over two years.
Look at a **cheaper flat** with Tom to lower monthly costs.
feel: She feels **calmer**, like getting a long notice period instead of a sacking.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long notice period instead of a sacking.
fieldNote: Even with ten years she stays anxious because her **income still ends** at the stove.
She trusts **laws with money**, citing her partner's paid bus training scheme.
She admits to **dropping courses** before, so finishing one matters to her.

steps.text: Study for a food hygiene qualification over two years
Push the union for a paid retraining fund
Look for a cheaper flat with Tom to cut rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have enough saved and Tom's job could go too. What would help is a law that makes owners pay into a retraining fund before the robots go in. And honestly, rent that doesn't eat half my pay.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people who aren't on the books. Half the kitchen porters in this town are cash in hand. Any notice period only counts if you're on paper, and plenty aren't.

headlineQuote: The people who own these machines shouldn't get all of it.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** sauté cook at a busy city bistro, renting a one-bed with her partner Tom.
She's a committed **union member** who never uses AI and sees new tools as unpaid extra work.
Her steady worries are **rent and hours**, so even the flat scenario leaves her uneasy.
She expects **pan robots** to end her cooking job, so the AGI scenarios turn her anxious or alarmed.
With more time she'd move toward **food hygiene** inspection, a job she believes stays human.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, with too little saved and her partner's job also at risk.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a law making owners pay into a **retraining fund** before robots go in.
She'd also be helped by **lower rent** that doesn't take half her pay.
